title: Difference between archaeology and history, with Indian examples
seo_title: Difference Between Archaeology and History Explained
meta_description: The difference between archaeology and history: sources, methods, time span and how the two work together, with Indian examples from Harappa to Ashoka.
summary: History studies the past mainly through written sources such as chronicles, letters, inscriptions and official records. Archaeology studies the past through material remains: tools, pottery, buildings, bones, seeds and soil layers. History is limited to societies that wrote; archaeology can reach the whole human past, and the two are strongest when used together.

sections.h2: Archaeology vs history: the short answer
paras: The difference lies in the evidence. A historian reads texts: royal chronicles, travellers' accounts, land grants, court records, newspapers. An archaeologist reads things: the debris of daily life buried in the ground, the walls of houses, the layout of a city, the food people threw away. Both are trying to understand people in the past, but they start from different material and use different methods.

In Indian universities the two often sit together, in departments of ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. That pairing reflects how closely they depend on each other for the Indian past, where many periods have few reliable texts and many texts have no fixed dates.

sections.h2: Sources: written records against material remains
paras: Historical sources were made to communicate. A king's inscription, a Mughal court history or a colonial survey report was written by someone with a purpose and an audience, and the historian's skill lies in reading it critically: who wrote it, for whom, and what they left out.

Archaeological sources were mostly never meant to say anything. A rubbish pit, a broken cooking pot or a blocked drain is an accidental record of behaviour. That makes it less biased in one sense, since nobody was trying to impress posterity, but harder to interpret, because objects do not explain themselves. The archaeologist has to work out meaning from context, association and comparison.

Some evidence sits on the border. Inscriptions and coins are texts, but they are also objects found in the ground. The specialist fields of [epigraphy](what-is-epigraphy.html) and [numismatics](what-is-numismatics.html) belong to both disciplines.

sections.h2: Time span: prehistory, protohistory and history
paras: Writing appears late in the human story. For most of the time humans have lived in South Asia, there are no texts at all, only stone tools, rock paintings and the remains of camps. This long stretch is prehistory, and archaeology is the only way to study it.

Indian scholars also use the term protohistory for cultures that had writing which we cannot yet read, such as the Harappans, or that are known from later texts but not their own. Everything we know about how Dholavira or Rakhigarhi worked comes from excavation, because the Indus script remains undeciphered.

The historical period in India is usually counted from the time of the earliest securely dated and readable inscriptions, Ashoka's edicts of the 3rd century BCE. Even then, archaeology keeps adding information that texts leave out.

sections.h2: Methods: the archive and the trench
paras: A historian works in libraries and archives, reading manuscripts, comparing versions of a text, checking dates and translating. An archaeologist works in the field and the laboratory: surveying, excavating, drawing sections, sieving soil, classifying pottery and sending samples for scientific dating. Our guide to [how an excavation works](how-an-excavation-works.html) walks through the field side.

Archaeology is also destructive in a way history is not. A manuscript can be read again; a layer, once dug, is gone. That is why archaeologists put so much effort into recording, and why excavation needs a permit. If you want to see what that feels like, a [practice excavation in a mock trench](mock-trench-a-practice-excavation.html) lets students dig and record without damaging a real site.

sections.h2: Where the two meet: Indian examples
paras: Ashoka is the clearest case. Later Buddhist texts told stories about a great king, but it was the decipherment of Brahmi in the 1830s and the reading of his rock and pillar edicts, found across the subcontinent, that turned him into a historical figure with his own voice. The texts are history; the stones that carry them were found and mapped through archaeology.

Elsewhere, excavation fills gaps texts leave. Sangam poems describe a world of trade and towns in the Tamil country, and excavations at sites such as Arikamedu near Puducherry and Keeladi near Madurai have given that world material form, from imported pottery to brick structures and inscribed potsherds.

Sometimes the two disagree, and that is useful. A chronicle may claim a city was founded by a particular king, while excavation shows people living there centuries earlier. Neither source automatically wins; the historian and archaeologist have to weigh both.

If you enjoy languages, reading old texts and arguing over interpretation, history may suit you. If you like fieldwork, objects, science and working in teams outdoors, archaeology may suit you better. In India the routes overlap: many archaeologists begin with a BA in history and specialise at MA level.

Our guide to [archaeology courses in India](archaeology-courses-in-india.html) sets out the options, and a career session on [archaeology after Class 12](archaeology-after-class-12.html) helps students and parents think through the choice.

faq.q: Is archaeology a part of history?
faq.a: Archaeology is a separate discipline with its own methods, but it is closely tied to history. In India it is usually taught within departments of ancient history, culture and archaeology, while in North America it is often part of anthropology. Both study the human past; they differ mainly in the kind of evidence they use.

faq.q: What are archaeological sources of history?
faq.a: Archaeological sources are material remains that help reconstruct the past: buildings, pottery, tools, ornaments, coins, inscriptions, seals, sculptures, human and animal bones, plant remains and the soil layers in which all these are found. In Indian history, inscriptions and coins are especially important for fixing dates and names of rulers.

Written history can be studied without excavation, but it would be poorer and often less reliable. Archaeology checks and adds to texts, especially for ordinary people, women, craftspeople and regions that texts ignore. For periods before writing, archaeology is the only source.

faq.q: Which came first, history or archaeology as a discipline?
faq.a: History writing is far older, going back to ancient chronicles. Archaeology as a systematic discipline developed in the 18th and 19th centuries. In India, organised archaeology began with the antiquarian work of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta from 1784 and the founding of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1861.

Neither is harder; they demand different skills. History needs close reading, languages and critical analysis of texts. Archaeology adds fieldwork, drawing, scientific methods and patience with fragmentary evidence. Students who enjoy both often do well in ancient Indian history, where the two are combined.

posts.hook: For most of human time in India, there was no writing at all.
posts.caption: Everything we know about those hundreds of thousands of years comes from archaeology: stone tools, rock paintings and the remains of camps. History, in the strict sense, starts very late.

posts.hook: Reading about a king? Ask what the ground says.
posts.caption: Texts tell you what someone wanted recorded. Excavation shows what people actually built, ate and threw away. When the two disagree, that is where the interesting questions start.

posts.hook: Can your students tell a text from a trench?
